papers.title: A coordinate-to-coordinate machine learning framework for contrast-agnostic brain target localization
papers.abstract: Representing a structure by a coordinate can be challenging particularly for structures which lack conspicuity, whether due to their small size, lack of contrast, or image artifact. In this paper, we developed a machine learning framework to localize brain targets from the coordinates of salient brain landmarks (i.e., coordinate-to-coordinate) that is agnostic to image contrast. We make use of a validated brain landmark annotation protocol inspired by classical stereotactic methods and a dataset which spans a wide range of MRI field strengths and neurodegenerative diseases. We apply this framework to predict deep brain stimulation targets, achieving an accuracy of 1-1.5 mm validated against expert rater annotations on ultra-high field (UHF) MRI. Results demonstrated comparable localization accuracy on test-retest data acquired using both standard and UHF MRI. Our proposed framework outperformed deformable registration on clinical MRI and performed comparably on multispectral UHF MRI. We deployed our model in the form of a website (stereotaxy.afids.io) and openly release all coordinate data. This framework is agnostic to MRI contrast and offers a method for rapid coordinate localization with applications more broadly in neuroimaging as well as for specialized settings like surgical planning.

papers.title: Synthetic Magnetic Resonance Spectra Generation using convex NMF in Neuro-Oncology
papers.abstract: Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy is a powerful, non-invasive technique for investigating the metabolic composition of biological tissues, particularly useful in the classification of brain tumours. However, its inclusion into machine learning pipelines is limited by the scarcity of large, labelled datasets. This work evaluates whether synthetic MR spectra generated using convex Non-negative Matrix Factorisation and probabilistic modelling of the resulting weight distributions can improve brain tumour classification. MR spectra from the INTERPRET database were decomposed into interpretable source and weight matrices, both separately for each of six diagnostic tasks and jointly across five tissue classes, at short and long echo time. Class-specific weight distributions were modelled using Gaussian Mixture Models and Kernel Density Estimation across a range of hyperparameter settings, and new weight vectors were sampled and recombined with the fixed source matrix to produce synthetic spectra; hyperparameters were selected by the mean squared error to the real class means. The diagnostic utility of the synthetic spectra was assessed with Linear Discriminant Analysis under three internal and four external evaluation strategies, the latter using an independent multi-centre cohort. Synthetic spectra were readily classified by models trained on real data (mean accuracy 0.87), but models trained on synthetic spectra alone generalised poorly, both to real INTERPRET spectra (0.55) and to the external cohort (0.47, against 0.84 for training on real data; p [≤] 0.003). Augmenting real training data with synthetic spectra neither improved nor significantly harmed external accuracy (mean paired differences between -0.04 and +0.01; all p [≥] 0.027 uncorrected, none significant after correction), and class-balanced augmentation did not help, and task-specific and joint decompositions performed comparably. The selected generative models were low in complexity and produced spectra closer to the class means than the real data are, suggesting that selection by reconstruction fidelity is poorly aligned with the goal of augmentation, and that internal validation alone would have overstated the value of the synthetic data.

papers.title: Centiloid Calibration and Application of MUSE-Based Amyloid PET Quantification for Florbetapir (AV-45)
papers.abstract: Introduction Amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) quantifies cerebral {beta}-amyloid in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but tracer- and processing-dependent variability limits comparability. We evaluated Centiloid transformations for multi-atlas segmentation (MUSE)-based [11C]Pittsburgh compound B (PiB) and [18F]florbetapir (AV-45) PET. Methods Standardized uptake value ratio (SUVr) Centiloid transformations without partial-volume correction (NoPVC) and with parallel level set regularization-based PVC (PLS-PVC) were calibrated using the original Klunk Centiloid PiB reference dataset (N = 79) and paired PiB-AV-45 Navitsky dataset (N = 43). Centiloid transformations were evaluated in Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; AV-45) and secondarily in Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (Knight-ADRC; PiB) cohorts. Outcomes included AD-cognitively normal (CN) separation and clinical associations. Scanner effects were examined in ADNI. Results MUSE-derived PiB SUVr measurements corresponded strongly with reference measurements (R2 = 0.963, ICC(A,1) = 0.981), and PiB-AV-45 cross-tracer correspondence was high (R2 = 0.873-0.884). NoPVC separated AD from CN in Knight-ADRC PiB (Hedges' g = 1.907) and ADNI AV-45 (g = 0.892). PLS-PVC yielded similar separation in Knight-ADRC ({Delta}g = -0.027; 95% CI -0.122 to 0.023) and modestly greater separation in ADNI ({Delta}g = 0.053; 95% CI 0.038-0.068). Scanner-associated variance represented 33.5% of total Centiloid variance in ADNI; on scanners other than one older model, AD-CN separation was larger (g = 1.31). Both approaches showed clinical associations. Discussion MUSE Centiloid transformations provide a framework for expressing PiB and AV-45 measurements in Centiloid units across independent cohorts. Scanner and processing differences warrant scanner-specific quality checks and cautious interpretation.

papers.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Assistance on Efficiency, Ergonomics, and Measurement Consistency of Abdominal Ultrasound
papers.abstract: OObjectives: Evaluate how the addition of AI-assisted image acquisition and measurements affects the efficiency, ergonomics, accuracy, and consistency of abdominal ultrasound examination. Methods: Randomized, crossover study utilizing an abdominal ultrasound system with integrated AI features. Experienced sonographers (N=33) performed standardized examinations with and without AI-assisted features enabled. Metrics of timing and control interactions by the non-scanning hand were acquired. Movements of the non-scanning hand were recorded during a subset of examinations (N=17) to evaluate distance traveled with and without AI. An offline measurement exercise (N=32) using standardized image datasets assessed agreement between AI-generated and manual measurements and the effect of AI assistance on the consistency of measurements across users. Results: AI assistance reduced mean exam time by 2.23 minutes (SD 0.44 minutes) (95% CI: -3.10, -1.36; P<0.001); independent of participants age, experience, or the sequence of AI-assisted vs manual scans. AI assistance reduced mean distance traveled by the non-scanning hand by 49.2% (P<0.001). AI assistance also reduced overall control interactions by the non-scanning hand by 36%, touchscreen reaches by 41.5%, interactions with the control panel by 23.4%, and mouse movements and clicks by 54.2% and 61.1%, respectively (P<0.001 for all). During offline measurement, users accepted 94.3% of AI-generated measures without modification. AI assistance reduced inter-user measurement variability by 74%. Conclusions: AI assistance significantly reduced exam time and improved ergonomics compared with manual scanning and supported more standardized measurements across users. These findings support the integration of AI-assisted tools into imaging workflows to enhance workflow efficiency, ergonomics, and diagnostic consistency.

papers.title: Interrater Reliability of Clinical Resting-State fMRI Network Classification: Comparison of Human Raters and an AI Algorithm
papers.abstract: Purpose Accurate classification of intrinsic brain networks is essential for the clinical interpretation of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), especially in complex pediatric populations. Manual classification of resting-state networks (RSNs) remains the clinical gold standard, yet variability among raters poses a challenge for reproducibility. This study aims to assess interrater reliability among five human raters and one AI algorithm. Methods Rs-fMRI data were collected from 269 scans in a clinical cohort predominantly composed of pediatric patients. Raters used an independent component analysis (ICA)-based pipeline to categorize RSNs into one of 13 categories. Percent agreement, Cohen's Kappa, and Fleiss's Kappa were used to measure agreement. Results Overall pairwise agreement for human-human pairs ranged from substantial to almost perfect ({kappa} = 0.655-0.845), while human-AI agreement ranged from fair to moderate ({kappa} = 0.289-0.401). Agreement was highest for Typical networks and Noise, whereas Atypical networks showed lower agreement, with moderate human-human agreement ({kappa} = 0.468-0.541) and poor-to-fair human-AI agreement ({kappa} = 0.147-0.305). Despite high human-human agreement on Noise components, human-AI kappa values for Noise were disproportionately low, a pattern that may reflect the high prevalence of Noise components and class imbalance in the model's training data. Conclusion Our findings underscore the need for standardized classification frameworks and targeted training to improve consistency, particularly for atypical networks. This study supports the development of reproducible rs-fMRI workflows and the potential use of AI as a complementary screening tool within clinical neuroimaging workflows.

papers.title: Adapting Echocardiographic Foundation Models for Detecting Pulmonary Embolism-Related Right-Heart Strain
papers.abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a time-sensitive medical emergency in which rapid recognition of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction by point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) can support early risk stratification. Here, we present HOPE (ecHO-Pulmonary Embolism), a real-world emergency cardiac POCUS video dataset comprising 4,069 patients with suspected PE, and EchoPE, a foundation-model-based video classification framework for detecting PE-associated right-heart phenotypes. HOPE includes five commonly acquired emergency echocardiographic views, with all positive PE cases confirmed by computed tomography pulmonary angiography. EchoPE builds on EchoPrime-pretrained echocardiographic representations and incorporates view recognition, task-specific adaptation, and attention-based interpretability. Experiments suggested that directly transferring EchoPrime representations to this disease-specific task provided limited performance, whereas EchoPE (AUROC 95.2 +/- 0.3) substantially outperformed both EchoPrime with a classification head (AUROC 87.6 +/- 1) and conventional video deep learning baselines. At a fixed sensitivity of 90%, EchoPE achieved a precision of 87.8, compared with 70.7 for EchoPrime. Among adaptation strategies, Low-Rank Adaptation combined with knowledge distillation provided the best balance between PE discrimination and preservation of pretrained echocardiographic semantics. Interpretability analyses showed that the adapted model focused on clinically relevant RV morphological changes, interventricular septal configuration, and informative temporal segments within ultrasound videos. Overall, HOPE and EchoPE demonstrate that echocardiographic foundation models require dataset-specific adaptation to identify PE-related right-heart strain and support the potential use of artificial intelligence-assisted bedside echocardiography for risk warning in acute care settings.

papers.title: Individualized Atypicality of Structure-Function Configuration Marks Subthreshold Depression in Adolescents
papers.abstract: BackgroundSubthreshold depression (StD) in adolescence represents a critical state preceding major depressive disorder, yet its neurobiological substrates remain poorly characterized. Conventional structure-function coupling rely on DTI tractography, which produces non-isomorphic matrices and unstable single-subject estimates, limiting their clinical utility. We developed a novel isomorphic and multi-omics framework to quantify individualized structure-function configurations and tested whether adolescents with StD show reproducible deviations from a group-mean reference in a validation sample. MethodsWe integrated five structural (cortical thickness, mean curvature, sulcal depth, fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity) and five functional (ReHo, ALFF, CBF, local and global connectivity strength) features to construct regional SIND-FIND configurations using symmetric KL divergence in a discovery-validation design (N = 131). Individual typicality scores were defined as the correspondence between each participants regional configuration profile and HC reference (Leave one out). The score has undergone parallel validations using conventional SC-FC coupling, molecular alignment (PET/AHBA), and behavioral correlations. ResultsGroup-mean configuration maps were spatially correlated across samples ({rho} = .93, pspin < .001). StD participants showed lower typicality than HC (F(1,94) = 8.73, p = .004); the conventional SC-FC comparison was not significant (F(1,92) = 3.31, p = .072). Regional differences involved frontoparietal and salience regions and aligned with PET (r = .55, pspin < .001) and AHBA (r = .47, pspin = .003) maps. After covariate adjustment, typicality correlated with SCL-90 ({rho} = -.262, q = .013), SDS ({rho} = -.234, q = .022), ISI ({rho} = -.296, q = .012) and PSQI ({rho} = -.288, q = .012; BH-FDR across five scales); coupling tracked depressive but not sleep symptoms (ISI {rho} = -.161, q = .124). Within validation StD participants, SCL-90 remained negatively associated with typicality ({rho} = -.42, p = .023). ConclusionOur isomorphic, multimodal framework captures coordinated structures-function deviation in adolescent StD with greater group-effect sensitivity than conventional SC-FC coupling, together with regional specificity, molecular spatial alignment, and behavioral relevance. Configuration typicality, defined relative to an HC group-mean reference, may serve as an individual-level marker of organizational deviation during adolescence, pending larger, demographic stratified samples.

papers.title: Within-scan MRI signal and texture in Alzheimer disease: a multicohort study
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Conventional MRI contains tissue signal and texture information beyond regional volume, but acquisition variability limits their comparability. We evaluated within-scan signal and texture analyses for estimating contemporaneous cognition and amyloid/tau burden in Alzheimer's disease (AD) beyond volumetry. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 2,437 baseline datasets from ADNI3, ADNI4, MCSA, SCAN/CLARiTI, and OASIS-3. SynthSeg defined regions for T1-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) measurements. Within-scan regional-to-rest log ratios (WSRLR) were compared with scanner-matched, cross-fitted cognitively normal (CN) references. Texture analysis used three-dimensional gray-level co-occurrence matrices (GLCM). Covariate-adjusted rank models examined associations; ADNI3-trained ridge, elastic-net, gradient-boosting, and TabPFN-v2 models were tested externally. RESULTS: Moderate-to-strong correlations were observed between regional signal changes assessed using WSRLR vs. CN-reference (cohort median regional rho=0.504-0.890; n=2,314). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and greater entropy were associated with AD dementia adjusted for volume, while opposite correlations were observed with the hippocampus (all q<0.001). Greater entorhinal FLAIR entropy correlated with lower Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores (r=-0.198 and -0.098, respectively; both q<0.001). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and T1 cluster shade were associated with higher regional tau uptake beyond volume and diagnosis (r=-0.146 and -0.205; both q<=0.010). Adding entorhinal and hippocampal signal and texture significantly improved pooled external MoCA (n=868) and MMSE (n=551) prediction in three of four models. DISCUSSION: Within-scan signal and texture demonstrated AD-related regional associations and improved prediction of contemporaneous cognitive performance beyond volumetry. Prospective validation is needed to evaluate their potential value in opportunistic dementia screening.

papers.title: Frontoparietal Hyperconnectivity as a Single-Subject Neural Signature of Chronic Tinnitus
papers.abstract: Chronic tinnitus, the persistent perception of phantom sound, affects 14 to 15% of adults yet lacks a validated neurophysiological biomarker, in part because group-average EEG analyses obscure the individual heterogeneity that defines the condition. In a multi-site case-control study of 544 participants (268 with tinnitus, mean age 45.4 {+/-} 16.1 years, 52% female) across seven independent international sites, we applied normative modelling to quantify how far each persons resting-state EEG deviates from age- and hearing-adjusted healthy norms. Fusing spectral-power and connectivity deviations, a classifier detected tinnitus with an area under the curve of 0.832 under site-grouped cross-validation of precomputed normative features. The single most discriminative feature, rank-stable across all seven sites, was theta-band right orbitofrontal (pars orbitalis) connectivity, which dominated attribution by roughly an order of magnitude. Theta hyperconnectivity spanned frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks while primary auditory cortex showed negligible involvement, favouring failed top-down gating over bottom-up auditory overactivity. Features identifying tinnitus presence were orthogonal to symptom severity. These findings reframe chronic tinnitus as a frontoparietal attention-network disorder and nominate right orbitofrontal theta hyperconnectivity as a site-robust diagnostic feature. Data were collected within the TIDE project (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06520865).

papers.title: Automated aortoiliac calcification segmentation from arterial-phase computed tomography scans: development and validation
papers.abstract: IntroductionArterial calcium is widely used as a biomarker for coronary artery disease but is underutilized in peripheral artery disease (PAD) due to challenges in automated measurement of peripheral vascular calcium. We developed a fully automated deep-learning pipeline for measurement of aortoiliac calcium from arterial-phase, contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic computed tomography angiography (CTA) to extract this important PAD biomarker. MethodsThe pipeline uses two nnU-Net models for aortoiliac arterial segmentation and identification of calcified voxels. We trained on 56 computed tomography (CT) scans and validated on 106 scans by comparing the pipelines calcium estimation from CTA against calcium burden on corresponding non-contrast phase CT within manually segmented arterial contours across a range of radiodensity thresholds (100-1000 Hounsfield units [HU]). Using the non-contrast HU threshold that maximized correlation between measures, we performed linear regression with five-fold cross-validation between pipeline-estimated and non-contrast calcium quantities, and risk reclassification analysis across quartiles using Monte Carlo simulations to compare pipeline and non-contrast-derived calcium burden quartiles while measuring quadratically weighted kappa. ResultsNon-contrast calcium burden calculated from voxels with attenuation [≥]400 HU correlated best with CTA calcium burden (Pearson r=0.952 for aortic calcium; Pearson r=0.955 for iliofemoral calcium) and was used for subsequent analysis. Five-fold cross-validation of non-contrast calcium volume prediction from pipeline-estimated CTA calcium burden, using [≥]400 HU to define non-contrast calcium voxels, demonstrated aggregated Pearson r>0.91 for all held-out folds in all three arterial regions tested. In risk reclassification analysis, quadratically weighted kappa for agreement between predicted and ground truth calcium quartile classifications was {kappa}=0.88 for the aorta, {kappa}=0.84 for bilateral iliofemoral arteries, and {kappa}=0.80 for all regions. ConclusionAortoiliac calcium burden can be accurately quantified from CTA with excellent reproducibility against calcium voxels [≥]400 HU on non-contrast imaging. Quantification of this important biomarker expands opportunities for improved peripheral vascular disease diagnosis and risk prediction. papers.title: Diffusion-based vertex-wise connectomics encodes individual differences in cognition, affect and pathology
papers.abstract: No two brains are wired alike, and much of a persons cognitive and clinical state is written in this individual variation, not in the group average. Structural connectomes, however, are typically read through group atlases that summarize connectivity into regional averages, leaving this individual signal untapped. We build a vertex-wise structural connectome, in which every cortical surface vertex is a node, and apply it across the Alzheimers continuum. Using an independent dataset for methodological development and a multisite cohort of 317 participants from ADNI-4, we show that connection distance and organizational scale form a nested hierarchy, from a long-range backbone to fine, short-range structure. The individual fingerprint is strongest in medium- and short-range connections and becomes less distinctive as connectivity is pooled into atlas parcels. This individual structure can be recovered across spatial scales, although its fidelity depends on diffusion acquisition quality, with multishell data providing a more informative reference than single-shell data. In the aging brain, an individually referenced balance between short- and long-range connectivity is associated with episodic memory, cognitive reserve, depressive symptoms, and shared molecular pathology. While cognitive associations largely reflect diagnostic differences, associations with depressive symptoms and pathology burden remain detectable after adjustment for diagnosis. These findings show that individual structural connectomes retain clinically and biologically relevant variation that is not fully captured by diagnostic classification or group-level summaries.

papers.title: Pulsed X-Ray CT with Temporally Aware Reconstruction for Three-Dimensional Endovascular Guidance: Phantom Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundEndovascular fluoroscopy provides limited depth information. Projection-level x-ray pulsing and prior-image reconstruction could enable volumetric CT updates from sparse projection data. PurposeTo assess whether pulsed sparse-view CT combined with temporally aware reconstruction could accurately localize robotically manipulated endovascular devices in a phantom. Materials and MethodsWe compared true pulsed acquisitions with matched retrospective sparsification (4-180 projections) in a modular phantom. Eight robotically generated device configurations in an anthropomorphic endovascular phantom were scanned with 1248 projections. Data were retrospectively sparsified to 6, 12, 24, 32, and 52 projections and reconstructed using filtered backprojection and a temporally aware prior-image method. Localization errors were measured relative to full-view filtered-backprojection measurements. Analyses were descriptive. ResultsMean CT number differences between true pulsed and matched retrospectively sparsified images were 4.8-6.2 Hounsfield units; corrected standard deviations were 27.5-29.9 Hounsfield units. Sparse-view filtered backprojection obscured device segments at 6 and 12 projections, whereas temporally aware reconstruction depicted both devices at all projection counts. At 6 projections, median centerline, guidewire-tip, and tip-to-vessel-wall errors were 0.82 mm (interquartile range, 0.10 mm), 0.71 mm (0.12 mm), and 0.03 mm (0.28 mm), respectively. All localization errors were below the 0.944-mm reconstructed voxel diagonal. ConclusionTrue pulsed and matched retrospectively sparsified acquisitions showed similar CT numbers in a modular phantom. In an anthropomorphic endovascular phantom, temporally aware reconstruction of retrospectively sparsified data localized robotically manipulated devices within one reconstructed voxel diagonal.

papers.title: Fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models and typed decisions for classifying findings in chest CT reports: paired English-Japanese internal testing and external testing on naturally written Japanese reports
papers.abstract: PurposeTo compare fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models (LLMs) and typed decisions (per-finding yes/no questions answered with a probability) for classifying 18 findings in chest CT reports, and to identify when typed decisions help. MethodsThis retrospective study used public data. The internal test set comprised 150 CT-RATE reports with paired Japanese translations at three quality levels; the external test set, 243 naturally written Japanese reports with human annotations (RR-Findings). We compared ModernBERT encoders fine-tuned on 20,444 reports, generative LLMs (gpt-6-luna, Qwen3.8-27B, MedGemma), and typed decisions with Jev, the Decisions API and Qwen. Thresholds fixed on 450 development reports were applied unchanged externally. The primary metric was micro-F1; case-level paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for 11 internal comparisons. ResultsEncoders were best internally (English 0.9853; radiologist-checked Japanese 0.9576) and exceeded Jev (differences 0.0367, 95% CI 0.0258-0.0484; 0.0336, 0.0215-0.0464). Externally, Jev (0.8844) lay within the encoder seed range (0.8656-0.9144), exceeded the three generative conditions tested externally (best 0.8564) and the Decisions API (0.8177), and had the smallest internal-to-external decrease (-0.0396). An encoder trained on 2,044 reports reached 0.8226 externally. Typed-versus-generated differences changed direction across models and test sets. At a fixed threshold of 0.5, Jev fell to 0.7753 externally. ConclusionFine-tuned encoders performed best with ample in-distribution labels. Although threshold-dependent, Jev, with thresholds fitted on only 450 labeled reports, fell within the encoder seed range externally and exceeded the generative LLMs and an encoder trained on 2,044 reports, making it an option when labels are scarce.

papers.title: Automated Gland MRI Radiomics for Predicting Time to Pathologic Progression during Prostate Cancer Active Surveillance
papers.abstract: BackgroundRepeated biopsies burden patients during prostate cancer active surveillance (AS). Existing MRI risk stratification tools avoiding biopsy remain limited by the difficulty of automated lesion segmentation. PurposeTo develop a model integrating gland MRI radiomics and clinicopathologic variables for predicting time to pathologic progression during prostate cancer AS. Materials and MethodsThis retrospective single-institution study included men with grade group 1 or favorable grade group 2 prostate cancer undergoing AS with fusion-targeted and systematic biopsy (2010-2025). Gland segmentation used nnU-Net; gland radiomic features were selected by LASSO-penalized survival regression to train an XGBoost accelerated failure time model. Comparator models were assessed by C-index, time-dependent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Kaplan-Meier, and decision curve analysis. ResultsOf 522 men (median age, 64 years [IQR, 59-68]), 410 were assigned by site to development and 112 to internal testing. Gland segmentation Dice was 0.89 {+/-} 0.04. The C-index was higher for the gland radiomics model (0.77) than for clinicopathologic (0.68) and lesion radiomics (0.68) models (adjusted P [≤] .017), with the highest time-dependent AUC at 36 months (0.87 [95% CI: 0.78, 0.94]). Progression-free survival was lower in high-risk than low-risk groups (36 months, 63.9% vs 100%; 48 months, 55.4% vs 93.8%; log-rank P < .001). At a 0.25 risk threshold, 49.1% and 31.3% were low risk at 36 and 48 months (negative predictive value, 1.00; positive predictive value, 0.36). ConclusionAn automated gland radiomics model predicted time to pathologic progression during AS better than clinicopathologic and lesion-based models.

papers.title: Longitudinal Multimodality Imaging of Cardiovascular Abnormalities Following Definitive Chemoradiation for Lung Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Background/ObjectivesCardiovascular complications following definitive chemoradiation therapy (CRT) for lung cancer are well recognized, but their longitudinal imaging manifestations remain incompletely characterized. We aimed to characterize cardiovascular abnormalities across multiple imaging modalities and electrocardiography during lung cancer survivorship. MethodsThis retrospective single-center study included patients treated with definitive CRT between 2013 and 2025 who underwent baseline and follow-up cardiovascular assessments. Findings from computed tomography, echocardiography, myocardial perfusion imaging, coronary angiography, and electrocardiography were categorized into exploratory, literature-informed cardiovascular phenotype domains across five follow-up intervals. Longitudinal patterns were evaluated using generalized estimating equations (GEE). and exploratory associations with clinical cardiovascular adverse events (CVAEs) were assessed using {chi}{superscript 2} or Fishers exact tests. ResultsEighty-six patients were included (mean age, 66 {+/-} 9.1 years; 46 women). Baseline coronary, thoracic aortic, and valvular calcification were common, affecting 72%, 88%, and 50% of patients, respectively. During the first 0-6 months, reduced LV systolic function (53%), valvular dysfunction (35%), and pericardial effusion (19%) were observed. Pericardial effusion was observed in 37% at 1-2 years, while calcification progression and pulmonary vascular abnormalities were identified during later follow-up intervals. Longitudinal analyses suggested positive associations between successive follow-up categories and calcification progression (average OR, 4.30), pulmonary artery enlargement (OR, 1.49; 95% CI, 1.10-2.02; P = 0.01), right-heart abnormalities (average OR, 1.65), and arrhythmia (OR, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.30-2.38; P < 0.001). Exploratory associations between imaging abnormalities and clinical CVAEs were also observed. ConclusionsLongitudinal multimodality cardiovascular assessments identified heterogeneous cardiovascular abnormalities across follow-up intervals following definitive CRT for lung cancer. Larger prospective studies are needed to validate these observations.

papers.title: Generative Deep Learning Maps Brain Oxygen Metabolism and Its Age-Related Decline from Two Standard Noninvasive MRI Scans
papers.abstract: PurposeTo develop a generative deep learning model mapping the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) from minimal, contrast-free MRI. Materials and MethodsThis retrospective study used 3-T MRI of healthy adults from one center (May 2015-June 2025). A conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) was trained to reproduce contrast-based analytical CMRO2 from progressively fewer quantitative MRI inputs (cerebral blood flow [CBF], T2*, T2, cerebral blood volume), T1-weighted MRI, or resting-state functional MRI. Models were trained on 54 participants and tested on 41 (25 women; mean age, 49 years {+/-} 23 [SD]), on calculation-task data, and, without retraining, on same-protocol (n = 24) and cross-vendor (n = 12) data. Agreement (r, mean absolute error [MAE]) was compared with the test-retest error of analytical CMRO2, and repeatability (n = 9) with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). ResultsA GAN using only CBF and T2* agreed with analytical CMRO2 as well as one adding T2 (r = 0.89 [95% CI: 0.88, 0.90] for both), with errors below the between-day test-retest error (median MAE, 38.1 vs 46.5 {micro}mol/100 g/min); CBF alone, T1-weighted MRI, and functional MRI performed worse (P [≤] .004). It was as repeatable as analytical CMRO2 (median ICC, 0.87 for both), preserved task-evoked patterns (Dice, 0.78), agreed with same-protocol (r = 0.89) and, less, cross-vendor data (r = 0.81; P [≤] .001), and captured the age-related decline (6.8 vs analytical, 5.0 {micro}mol/100 g/min per decade). ConclusionGenerative deep learning mapped brain oxygen metabolism from two contrast-free scans with repeatability comparable to the reference.

papers.title: Is Latin American brain anatomy "normal"? Construction and evaluation of a Chilean brain template
papers.abstract: Many neuroimaging processes use a brain reference anatomical template; the most widely used is the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template. Yet studies have shown that different populations exhibit different global brain features, and the use of a unique Canadian template may introduce biases in analyses for other populations. The purpose of this work is to construct a brain template that accurately represents our local population in Chile. In addition, our project explicitly addresses another pressing challenge: the limited availability of high-field MR scanners in Latin America. In this context, we will build our template using a 0.55T MR scanner, thus ensuring not only population specificity but also methodological alignment with the technological realities of our healthcare systems. Healthy volunteers (n = 76, ages 18-60) underwent T1-weighted MRI. Images were preprocessed and iteratively registered via rigid and non-linear steps to generate a Chilean template (CL76). Evaluation involved dimensional comparisons with Canadian, Indian, Chinese, and Korean templates. Deformation metrics were estimated for an additional 23 volunteers. The Chilean template measures 166 x 132 x 100 mm3, smaller than the Canadian one (179 x 137 x 118 mm3), and has distinct proportions, particularly the width/height ratio of 1.31 versus 1.16. Deformation of a test population onto CL76 was significantly lower (p = 0.010) and less variable than that of MNI152. The top deformed regions onto CL76 or onto MNI152 differed, confirming population specificity on the template. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first brain template generated in South America; however, we do not claim to represent the entire continent--only a specific population from Chile. This work highlights the need for broader representation across diverse populations, particularly to counterbalance the current over-representation of individuals from high-income countries with established research and imaging infrastructures.

papers.title: Lightweight and Explainable AI for Chest Radiograph Classification in Low-Resource Settings: Cross-Dataset Generalization, Grad-CAM Verification, and Uncertainty-Aware Referral
papers.abstract: Chest radiography is the most common imaging test worldwide, yet models trained on one hospitals data often fail elsewhere, a critical problem for low-resource hospitals that cannot collect large local datasets. This paper presents a lightweight, explainable framework for chest radiograph classification, trained and evaluated entirely on CPU with public data. EfficientNet-B0 and ResNet-18 are trained on a 10,000-image subset of NIH ChestX-ray14 and evaluated without retraining on a paediatric pneumonia set, alongside a TorchXRayVision DenseNet121 pretrained baseline and a model trained directly on paediatric data. On the NIH test set (n = 2,500), the best single model reaches pneumonia AUC-ROC 0.738 and a two-model ensemble 0.742, while an adult-trained model falls to AUC 0.454 on paediatric images, and, symmetrically, a paediatric-trained model falls to 0.473 on adult NIH images. Pooling the adult and paediatric training sets into one binary pneumonia model changes the picture: a merged EfficientNet-B0 reaches AUC 0.951 (95% CI 0.932-0.967) on paediatric images, the first result whose whole 95% CI clears 0.90, and 0.675 on NIH images with zero sensitivity at threshold 0.5, while a merged ResNet-18 reaches 0.962 on paediatric and 0.606 on NIH images. Pooling fixes the catastrophic cross-domain failure but does not recover adult-only performance, and ensembling a merged model with a single-domain model adds nothing on either test set. Grad-CAM heatmaps are shown for true positives, false negatives and false positives, and Monte Carlo dropout referral raises answered-case accuracy from 0.889 to 0.948 on NIH data but not under domain shift. All results carry bootstrap confidence intervals, and the limits of a 22-positive NIH test set are stated plainly.

papers.title: Blood acceleration metric: A potential surrogate for fractional flow reserve to assess the functional severity of carotid artery stenosis
papers.abstract: Purely morphological assessment of an arterial stenosis is not sufficient to adequately evaluate its functional significance. The metric of fractional flow reserve (FFR) is the gold standard for assessing coronary artery stenoses. However, the risks associated with catheterization and induction of hyperemia needed to measure FFR impede its application to cerebral vessels. Approaches based on a combination of computed tomography (CT) with computer simulations have been proposed to address this issue, yielding an estimate of fractional flow reserved (FFRCT). While promising, they are time-consuming and difficult to integrate into established clinical workflows. Here, we propose a new, easily derivable parameter termed the blood acceleration metric (BAM). It incorporates readily measurable morphological and hemodynamic features, such as minimum stenosis diameter and peak systolic velocity, to assess the functional severity of carotid artery stenoses. Preliminary assessment on 27 mild to moderate stenoses indicates a strong negative correlation (R=-0.85) between BAM and FFRCT. BAM should be further evaluated as a potential surrogate for FFR and, thereby, as a possible predictor of stroke risk.

papers.title: Manifestation-Guided Adaptation of CT Foundation Model for Early Neurological Prognosis after ECPR
papers.abstract: PurposeTo develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. MethodsThis retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean {+/-} SD across five held-out folds. ResultsOf 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 {+/-} 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 {+/-} 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 {+/-} 0.037), specificity (93.7% {+/-} 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% {+/-} 9.2%. ConclusionManifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.

papers.title: Anatomy-Aware 3D GAN with Local Mask Refinement for Brain MRI Inpainting
papers.abstract: Brain tumor MRI inpainting aims to synthesize plausible healthy-appearing tissue in regions removed from pathological scans. We present an anatomy-aware three-dimensional generative adversarial network for Task 4 of the BraTS 2026 challenge. The method combines mask-aware gated convolutions, mirrored contralateral context, attention-modulated skip fusion, boundary-aware refinement, and a local masked-region refiner, each adapted from established components in the image synthesis and inpainting literature. The model is trained with a two-stage objective that first emphasizes voxel-wise and structural reconstruction and then applies low-weight adversarial fine-tuning. On a deterministic local held-out split, the proposed method substantially improves over a simple 3D AutoEncoder baseline but does not surpass the challenges Pix2Pix3D baseline. On the official BraTS 2026 Task 4 evaluation server, the submitted model obtained a mean SSIM of 0.658 and a mean PSNR of 14.81 dB over 219 evaluated cases, lower than the local held-out figures. We report these results transparently, analyze likely contributing factors, and identify the controlled ablations (removal of the mirrored-context channel and of the two-stage schedule) required to isolate the contribution of each architectural component.

papers.title: Biomechanical characterization of head and neck tumors and corresponding lymph nodes for nodal assessment by ultrasound shear wave elastography and MR elastography
papers.abstract: BackgroundMalignant remodeling alters tissue mechanics, but biomechanical differences among primary head and neck tumors, benign cervical lymph nodes, and nodal metastases remain poorly characterized. We used in vivo and ex vivo ultrasound shear-wave elastography (USE) and ex vivo tabletop MR elastography (ttMRE) to compare stiffness, viscoelasticity, and spatial heterogeneity across these tissue groups and to assess cross-modal agreement. As a secondary objective, we explored whether primary-tumor biomechanics differed by pathological nodal status. MethodsEighteen patients - 17 with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) and one with salivary duct carcinoma - underwent surgical resection. Target cervical lymph nodes were assessed by in vivo USE, and resected lymph nodes and primary tumors by ex vivo USE. Multifrequency ttMRE was successfully performed in 8 benign lymph nodes, 8 metastatic lymph nodes, and 13 primary tumors and yielded shear modulus , power-law exponent , and spatial heterogeneity metrics. Quantitative T1, T2, fat-fraction, and apparent-diffusion-coefficient (ADC) measurements were also performed. Group comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis tests with Dunn-Bonferroni post-hoc tests, paired comparisons used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and primary tumors from node-positive versus node-negative patients were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests. Diagnostic performance was summarized by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and cross-modal agreement by Spearman correlation. ResultsBy ttMRE, benign lymph nodes were softer than metastatic lymph nodes and primary tumors (median [IQR], 3.4 [3.1-8.9] vs 57.3 [26.2-102.4] vs 24.2 [13.2-37.6] kPa; p = 0.001) with more homogeneous texture as indicated by lower stiffness entropy (H(), 1.24 [1.05-1.30] vs 1.88 [1.71-2.27] vs 1.70 [1.56-1.78] nats; p = 0.002). Although the unpaired distributions of metastatic nodes and primary tumors overlapped, matched within-patient comparisons showed higher stiffness in primary tumors than in benign nodes and in metastatic nodes than in their corresponding primary tumors (n = 6 pairs per comparison; p = 0.031 for each). For discriminating metastatic from benign lymph nodes, AUC was 0.97 for ttMRE , 0.96 for in vivo USE, and 0.90 for ex vivo USE. By ttMRE, primary tumors from node-positive patients had lower stiffness than those from node-negative patients (12.1 [10.2-16.1] vs 30.1 [26.4-72.8] kPa; uncorrected p = 0.035), whereas ex vivo USE did not show differences (p = 0.415). ttMRE correlated with ex vivo USE ({rho} = 0.70, p < 0.001) and in vivo ({rho} = 0.69, p = 0.003). ConclusionIn our prospective cohort, tissue stiffness was the main biomechanical feature distinguishing benign from metastatic cervical lymph nodes. Furthermore, an association between lower primary-tumor stiffness and pathological nodal positivity was observed by MRE but not USE. Our findings establish a proof of concept for the biomechanical characterization of primary head and neck tumors and regional lymph nodes.

papers.title: Deep-learning body composition analysis of routine CT robust to scan range, slice order and contrast phase
papers.abstract: PurposeTo develop and validate a fully automated pipeline that measures skeletal muscle and adipose tissue at L1 and L3 on routine CT with varied scan ranges, slice orders and contrast phases, rejects levels outside the scan and converts measures to non-contrast equivalents. Materials and methodsThe pipeline (sarco) combines orientation detection, L1/L3 localisation with out-of-range rejection, U-Net segmentation, six-class contrast-phase estimation, phase-specific conversion to non-contrast-equivalent values and, as an auxiliary output, muscle and marrow age estimation. We evaluated it on five single-centre datasets (4986 series): agreement with radiologist-corrected labels using five-fold cross-fitting (2025 series), artificially truncated scans, contrast-enhanced series paired with non-contrast series of the same examination, and the prognostic value of fully automated measures in 2006 patients after curative cancer surgery. TotalSegmentator served as a comparator. ResultsOn held-out folds, L3 skeletal muscle area (SMA) agreed with the reference (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.983; bias +1.35 cm{superscript 2}). On truncated scans processed with cross-fitted localisation models, the chosen L3 slice was off by half a vertebra or more in 4.7-5.6% of volumes (TotalSegmentator 11.3-14.3%). Four-group phase accuracy was 0.949, exceeding TotalSegmentator in scans shorter than 400 mm (0.952-0.960 vs 0.643-0.668), and conversion reduced the root mean square error of L3 muscle attenuation against the same-examination non-contrast series from 7.96 to 2.81 HU. Combined age estimates had a mean absolute error of 6.5 years. Automatically measured low muscle mass increased the cross-validated Unos C of the baseline model by 0.034 (95% CI 0.009-0.053; cancer-specific survival) and 0.031 (0.016-0.048; overall survival), whereas converted L3 muscle attenuation added 0.012 (-0.005 to 0.024) for overall survival. ConclusionThe pipeline provides robust, contrast-phase-aware body composition measures from routine CT with varied scan ranges and reproduces known prognostic associations without manual input. Short abstractWe validated a fully automated pipeline for L1/L3 body composition on routine CT. It handled truncated scans, estimated the contrast phase, converted measures to non-contrast equivalents, agreed closely with radiologist-corrected labels and reproduced prognostic associations in 2006 surgical patients.

papers.title: Bootstrapping surgeon labeling campaigns with x0-diffusion: label-efficient vessel segmentation of catheter-based angiograms
papers.abstract: ObjectiveAssess which architecture is the most label-efficient for vessel segmentation of catheter-based angiograms, and whether a diffusion model trained with extreme data scarcity could serve as a scaffold for expert annotation. Materials and Methodsx0-diffusion, SAM, DeepLabV3, ResNet-UNet, ViT-DPT, and ResNet-ViT hybrid were compared at 16, 32, and 80 labeled images from the 500-image Dr-SAM dataset under 5x5-fold repeated cross-validation, using one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. A vascular surgeons annotation time, from scratch and when correcting x0-diffusion predictions, was also measured. ResultsAt 16 training images, x0-diffusion achieved the highest Dice (0.882) and IoU (0.795) of the six models, outperforming every competitor in all 25 paired runs on Dice, by 0.047 over zero-shot SAM and 0.226 over DeepLabV3. The advantage narrowed as labels increased: at 32 images x0-diffusion was not significantly different from the two strongest convolutional models, and at 80 images those models scored marginally higher (0.923 and 0.920 vs. 0.910). Correcting 16-image x0-diffusion predictions on five test angiograms averaged 11.1 surgeon-minutes per image versus 20.6 from scratch. DiscussionThe advantage of x0-diffusion is label efficiency, not peak accuracy, with the strongest convolutional models needing twice the labels to match it. It rarely fails where zero-shot SAM fails, so at the start of an annotation campaign, correcting its predicted masks could cut surgeon annotation time by an estimated 37 to 45%. ConclusionWith very few labels, x0-parameterized diffusion is the strongest vessel segmenter tested and a candidate scaffold for expert annotation. Layman SummarySegmenting vessels on an angiogram manually takes a vascular surgeon about twenty minutes per image. This study shows that an x0-diffusion model trained on only 16 angiograms draws outlines good enough to correct rather than redraw, which took the surgeon about half as long on five test images.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for pulmonary tuberculosis detection on chest X-ray images: A systematic review and diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based computer-aided detection (CAD) of tuberculosis (TB) on chest X-ray (CXR) may standardize screening and triage in settings with few radiologists but its accuracy in clinical cohorts remains uncertain. We searched five databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, OpenAlex, Lens.org) on 15 March 2026 for studies published between January 2020 and March 2026, and we appraised these studies using QUADAS-2. Evaluations from clinical cohorts with complete 2 x 2 data and a microbiological or composite reference standard for all participants were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, with 95% prediction intervals. We accounted for overlapping participants by performing a post hoc analysis with one evaluation per cohort and used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence. No protocol was prepared or registered. We included 21 studies (26 evaluations of AI models). Nine evaluations from three independent cohorts were pooled. Pooled sensitivity was 0.896 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.874 to 0.915, prediction interval 0.798 to 0.950) and pooled specificity was 0.689 (95% CI 0.642 to 0.732; prediction interval 0.499 to 0.831). Both confidence intervals include the World Health Organization (WHO) triage thresholds (sensitivity 90%, specificity 70%). When a screening study with partial verification was added, pooled specificity increased to 0.735. Eighteen of 24 assessed evaluations were at high risk of bias and only 1 of 21 studies was prospective, fully verified, externally validated and met the WHO thresholds. Certainty of evidence was low for sensitivity and very low for specificity. A subsequent PubMed search found additional eligible clinical evaluations that were not screened, so the review is incomplete for those studies. In clinical cohorts, AI-CXR sensitivity is close to the WHO triage target, and specificity is close to, but not clearly above, its target. The evidence is pooled across only three cohorts, and specificity varies by product and setting. Thresholds need to be calibrated locally, and prospective, externally validated evaluations are needed before widespread deployment.

papers.title: Middle Temporal Gyrus Neurite Microstructure and Scam Susceptibility in Older Adults Without Dementia
papers.abstract: BackgroundFinancial exploitation is a prevalent public health concern among older adults, and emerging evidence links vulnerability to gray matter macrostructure and white matter microstructure, including within brain regions and networks implicated in early Alzheimers disease. Although diffusion tensor imaging is sensitive to age-related variation in brain microstructure, its scalar metrics cannot distinguish among the tissue properties contributing to observed differences. Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) models distinct tissue compartments, yielding estimates of neurite density, dendritic complexity, and extracellular free water. MethodsThis study examined associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics using ultra-high-field 7-Tesla imaging in 116 older adults without dementia. Neurite density index (NDI), orientation dispersion index (ODI), and free-water fraction were quantified within seven a priori regions of interest linked to early Alzheimers disease. Multivariate regressions evaluated associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics, adjusting for age, sex, education, and global cognition, with multiple comparison correction within each metric. For significant regions, post-hoc hierarchical regression models tested whether NODDI metrics explained variance beyond regional cortical thickness, total gray matter, and total intracranial volume. ResultsGreater scam susceptibility was associated with higher NDI ({beta}=0.30, pFDR=.025) and lower ODI ({beta}=-0.28, pFDR=.044) in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG). No other regions survived correction. Additionally, MTG NDI and ODI explained variance beyond macrostructure measures. ConclusionsThese findings identify NODDI metrics as novel microstructural correlates of scam susceptibility beyond macrostructure, supporting investigation of their relevance to financial vulnerability in older age.

papers.title: Volumetric Analysis of the Deltoid Muscle From Neck-to-Knee Dixon MRI: A pilot population assessment of a posterior intramuscular injection target
papers.abstract: BackgroundDeltoid muscle volume varies across anatomical regions and population groups, with potential implications for intramuscular injection site selection. Evidence comparing middle and posterior deltoid volumes in vaccine-eligible populations is limited. PurposeTo compare middle and posterior deltoid muscle volumes by vaccine eligibility group, sex, and side. MethodsDeltoid muscles were manually segmented into anterior, middle and posterior regions in 43 UK Biobank Dixon MRI scans. A MONAI deep learning model trained on the annotations (Dice score = 0.78) segmented deltoid muscles of 5,239 participants, categorised by UK flu vaccination eligibility: A ([≥]65 years without risk conditions, n=1,760), B ([≥]65 with risk conditions, n=1,744), and C (<65 with risk conditions, n=1,735). Bilateral-average posterior and middle volumes were compared using a paired t-test. A linear mixed-effects model assessed posterior-middle differences by group, sex and side. ResultsMean age was 66.7 {+/-} 7.2 years and body mass index was 27.5 {+/-} 5.7 kg/m2 (mean {+/-} SD). Posterior deltoid volume exceeded the middle deltoid volume by 55.36 ml (95% CI, 54.14-56.58, p<0.0001). Posterior-middle differences were largest in Group A, followed by B and then C, greater in men, and greater on the right side (all p<0.0001). Mean segmentation-quality score was 4.27 {+/-} 0.73 on a five-point Likert scale and weighted inter-observer kappa was 0.583 (95% CI, 0.452 - 0.713). ConclusionsAmong individuals eligible for the UK flu immunisation, posterior deltoid volume was greater than middle deltoid volume. These findings support further anatomical assessment of the posterior deltoid as a potentially safer injection target. Key ResultsO_LIThe deltoid muscles of 5,239 participants from the UK Biobank matching UK annual influenza vaccination eligibility were segmented using a deep learning-based model, enabling precise volumetric quantification of the anterior, middle and posterior deltoids. C_LIO_LIThe posterior deltoid demonstrated a larger average muscle volume when compared to the middle volume across vaccine-eligible groups and sexes (p<0.0001). C_LIO_LIThese findings provide a comprehensive reference framework for deltoid assessment across different ages and genders, enhancing both research and clinical decision-making for IM injection site selection. C_LI Summary statementAutomated deltoid volumetry in a pilot UK Biobank cohort revealed greater posterior than middle deltoid volume, supporting further evaluation of the posterior deltoid for a potential alternative intramuscular vaccination site.

papers.title: Silent Drift and Site-level Variance in Clinical AI: Real-world performance and subgroup analysis for post-market monitoring of an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for high-risk use case of pulmonary embolism
papers.abstract: BackgroundFDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for pulmonary embolism (PE) detection has been widely used; however, its performance has not been analyzed for subgroups, clinical sites, and temporal stability. MethodsThis retrospective, six-site health system study evaluated the Aidoc BriefCase PE triage model (K190072) across 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) examinations between July 2023 and March 2026. Reference-standard PE characteristic labels were extracted from radiology reports using a zero-shot LLM pipeline validated against a radiologist-annotated 600 reports ({kappa} =0.98). Model performance was evaluated across demographics, embolus characteristics, and site. Temporal behavior was evaluated on operating point by logistic regression, with and without site adjustment, and by segmented regression. ResultsPE was present in 1,402/14,736 examinations (9.5%). Overall sensitivity was 64.1% (95% CI, 61.5-66.6%), specificity 98.8% (95% CI, 98.6-99.0%), compared with 93% sensitivity and 93.7% specificity in the FDA 510(k) summary. Sensitivity fell with peripherality (central 88.6%, lobar or segmental 63.1%, subsegmental 33.3%) and with chronicity (acute 65.5%, chronic 57.4%). Sensitivity differed significantly between the two highest-volume sites, 68.7% and 55.7% (P < .001), with CT scanner as the only variable different between the two sites. The false-positive rate fell 40% per year (P<.001) at a similar rate at two sites, while sensitivity fell 15% per year at site A (P<.036), from 72.5% to 65.0% between two halves of the study period. The manufacturer did not report model updates or threshold changes during the study period. ConclusionsDeployed sensitivity was substantially below the cleared benchmark and varied 13 points by site. The gradual shift in high specificity at the cost of low sensitivity, either from data drift or threshold change, either not monitored or not documented by the manufacturer, highlights the importance of independent continuous post-market monitoring.

papers.title: LungAI: An AI Biomarker that Refines Lung-RADS v2022 Triage of Screen-Detected Pulmonary Nodules
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe Lung-RADS algorithm standardizes the management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules, but its risk assessment is driven chiefly by nodule size and attenuation. This misallocates a meaningful fraction of patients: a nontrivial share of small malignancies receive 12-month surveillance while large benign nodules proceed to invasive workup. Artificial intelligence (AI) may supply risk information independent of the imaging features Lung-RADS already uses. MethodsWe validated LungAI, an investigational deep learning nodule malignancy classifier not yet cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), on the held-out NLST test partition of Ardila et al. (2,747 low-dose CT examinations from 1,244 patients with [≥]1 solid or part-solid 4-30 mm nodule; 89 pathologically confirmed cancers, prevalence 3.2%). We compared discrimination against Sybil, mean nodule diameter, and estimated nodule volume. A board-certified radiologist assigned Lung-RADS v2022 categories to a positives-enriched random subset (226 eligible examinations; 78 cancers), projected to the full cohort by contingency weighting. A per-category reclassification algorithm shifted patients along the existing Lung-RADS management ladder using a-priori score cutpoints. We evaluated a separately locked follow-up configuration on examinations with a prior scan. ResultsLungAI achieved AUROC 0.92 (95% CI 0.88-0.95) and AUPRC 0.47 (0.35-0.61), outperforming Sybil ({Delta}AUROC 0.07; {Delta}AUPRC 0.18), diameter ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.34), and volume ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.38; all P<0.001). Against Lung-RADS v2022 scored ordinally on the weighted annotated subset, LungAI improved AUPRC ({Delta}AUPRC 0.31, P=0.003) but not AUROC ({Delta}AUROC 0.03, P=0.20). LungAI added discriminative information independent of diameter (likelihood-ratio {chi}2=161, P<10-36; {Delta}AUROC 0.10) and, on follow-up examinations, independent of delta diameter, volume doubling time, and new-nodule status ({chi}2=79, P<10-18). Integrated with Lung-RADS, LungAI reduced cancers on the slowest (12-month rescan) pathway by 46% (3.1[->]1.6 per 1,000 examinations) and benign biopsy referrals by 20% (32.7[->]26.2 per 1,000 examinations) at approximately unchanged total biopsy volume (51.0[->]50.1 per 1,000). Assuming full adherence to recommended follow-up, the combined approach yielded 25 months of net diagnostic lead time, an estimated net cost saving of [~]$2,200, and 6.5 fewer benign biopsies per 1,000 examinations; accounting for published adherence rates, it yielded 1.6 additional cancer diagnoses within 1 year per 1,000 examinations. ConclusionsLungAI contributes malignancy-risk information orthogonal to the size- and growth-based features underlying Lung-RADS and improves the allocation of screening patients across the existing management spectrum while potentially decreasing invasive procedures for benign lesions. Multi-site, multi-geography validation is required to demonstrate practical generalizability.

papers.title: WALRUS: Robust and Transferable Deep Learning for Water and Lipid Removal in 1H-MRSI
papers.abstract: Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (1H-MRSI) enables non-invasive mapping of brain metabolism, but reliable quantification is challenged by residual water and extracranial lipid contamination. Recent work demonstrated that a deep learning model trained on simulated metabolite spectra combined with in vivo-derived water and lipid signals can outperform conventional nuisance-removal methods. However, this approach relied on heuristic simulation parameter distributions and a subject-specific L2-derived lipid estimate as an auxiliary network input, requiring subject-specific lipid masks and L2 processing during inference. Here, we introduce WALRUS (Water And Lipid Removal Using Spectral Learning), a fitting-consistent and empirically calibrated framework developed through a systematic evaluation of simulation realism, architectural priors, and network optimization. WALRUS uses the same metabolite basis as downstream spectral fitting and calibrates deliberately broadened simulation distributions from in vivo measurements. Controlled 7 T experiments demonstrate that empirical simulator calibration substantially improves nuisance removal and metabolite quantification compared with heuristic training distributions. With the optimized simulator, a capacity-matched comparison reveals no clear additional benefit from the L2-derived prior, allowing its removal and substantially simplifying inference. Further improvements are achieved with the final higher-capacity U-Net, while on-the-fly simulation improves generalization compared with training on a fixed synthetic dataset. The same framework was subsequently recalibrated and retrained at 3 T, where WALRUS outperformed conventional HLSVD+L2 processing on held-out data. Together, WALRUS combines these advances into an optimized framework that improves nuisance removal and downstream metabolite fitting, requires no subject-specific lipid segmentation or L2-derived auxiliary input during inference, and can be systematically adapted to different acquisition settings.
